items.back: $f(E)=\{f(x): x∈E\}$, $f^{−1}(G)=\{x: f(x)∈G\}$. Preimages commute with unions, intersections and complements; images only with unions.
$A$ is countable if $A \sim N$ (a bijection exists), at most countable if finite or countable, uncountable otherwise.
A set $X$ with $d:X×X→ℝ$ such that $d(p,q)>0$ for $p≠q$, $d(p,p)=0$, $d(p,q)=d(q,p)$, and $d(p,q) ≤ d(p,r)+d(r,q)$.
$\{q : d(p,q)<r\}$, the open ball of radius $r>0$.
$p$ is a limit point of $E$ if every neighborhood of $p$ contains a point $q≠p$ of $E$. A point of $E$ that is not a limit point is isolated. The set of limit points is $E'$.
$E$ is closed if $E'⊂E$. $p$ is interior if some $N_{r}(p)⊂E$. $E$ is open if every point is interior.
Perfect: closed with no isolated points ($E=E'$). Bounded: inside some ball. Dense in $X$: every point of $X$ is in $E$ or is a limit point of $E$.
items.classNote: Dense (L4.2) and bounded (L5.1) done; perfect not yet.

items.back: $\bar E = E ∪ E'$.
$E⊂Y⊂X$ is open relative to $Y$ if each $p∈E$ has an $r$ with $N_{r}(p)∩Y ⊂ E$.
$K$ is compact if every open cover of $K$ has a finite subcover.
$A,B$ are separated if $A∩\bar B$ and $\bar A ∩ B$ are empty. $E$ is connected if it is not a union of two nonempty separated sets.
Every infinite subset of a countable set is countable.
A union of countably many countable sets is countable. Corollary: an at-most-countable union of at-most-countable sets is at most countable.
items.note: Quiz 2 problems 2 and 14 are both this theorem in disguise.

items.back: If $A$ is countable, so is $A^{n}$. Corollary: $ℚ$ is countable.
The set of all sequences of 0s and 1s is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal process). Hence $ℝ$ is uncountable.
Every $N_{r}(p)$ is an open set.

items.front: Limit points see infinitely many points
items.back: If $p$ is a limit point of $E$, every neighborhood of $p$ contains infinitely many points of $E$. Corollary: finite sets have no limit points.
$E$ is open iff $E^{c}$ is closed. Corollary: $F$ is closed iff $F^{c}$ is open.
Any union of open sets is open; any intersection of closed sets is closed. Finite intersections of open sets are open; finite unions of closed sets are closed.
$\bar E$ is closed; $E=\bar E$ iff $E$ is closed; $\bar E ⊂ F$ for every closed $F⊇E$.
items.note: Quiz 2 problem 10 uses the last one.

items.back: If $E⊂ℝ$ is nonempty and bounded above, $\sup E∈\bar E$. So $\sup E∈E$ when $E$ is closed.
$E$ is open relative to $Y$ iff $E=Y∩G$ for some open $G⊂X$.
For $K⊂Y⊂X$, $K$ is compact relative to $X$ iff compact relative to $Y$.
items.note: Unlike openness, compactness does not depend on the ambient space.

items.back: Compact subsets of metric spaces are closed. Closed subsets of compact sets are compact.
items.classNote: Class proof of “compact ⇒ closed” covers $K$ by the open sets $\{p : d(p,x)>1/n\}$.

items.back: If every finite subfamily of a family of compact sets has nonempty intersection, the whole family does. Corollary: nested nonempty compact sets have nonempty intersection.
If $E$ is an infinite subset of compact $K$, then $E$ has a limit point in $K$.
items.classNote: Stated as “$K⊂ℝ^{k}$ is compact iff every infinite subset has a limit point in $K$” (true in any metric space); not proved yet.

items.back: Nested closed intervals (or $k$-cells) have nonempty intersection. Every $k$-cell is compact.
items.classNote: Nested intervals proved with $x=\sup a_{n}$; the bisection proof that cells are compact was done for $k=1$.

items.back: For $E⊂ℝ^{k}$ these are equivalent: $E$ is closed and bounded; $E$ is compact; every infinite subset of $E$ has a limit point in $E$.
items.classNote: Class proof: a bounded set sits in some $N_{R}(x)$, which sits in a $k$-cell; closed subsets of compact sets are compact.
items.note: The first equivalence fails in general metric spaces.

items.back: Every bounded infinite subset of $ℝ^{k}$ has a limit point in $ℝ^{k}$.
items.classNote: Proved by putting the set inside a compact $k$-cell. Discrete-metric example shows it fails in general metric spaces.

items.back: A nonempty perfect set in $ℝ^{k}$ is uncountable. Corollary: every interval $[a,b]$ ($a<b$) is uncountable.
Remove open middle thirds forever. The result is compact, nonempty, perfect (so uncountable), and contains no interval.
$E⊂ℝ$ is connected iff whenever $x,y∈E$ and $x<z<y$, then $z∈E$ (i.e. $E$ is an interval).
$X\sim Y$ if a bijection exists; $\sim$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Examples: $2N$ and $ℤ$ are countable.
If $f:A→B$ is one-to-one and $B$ is finite (countable), then $A$ is finite with $\#A≤\#B$ (at most countable). If $f$ is onto and $A$ is finite (countable), so is $B$ (at most countable).
items.note: The onto case uses a right inverse $g$ with $f∘g=\mathrm{id}$.

items.back: $(n,m)↦2^{n}3^{m}$ is one-to-one (unique factorization). The Cantor pairing $f(n,m)=\tfrac{(n+m−2)(n+m−1)}{2}+n$ is a bijection onto $N$.
$\bigcup_{α}E_{α}$ and $\bigcap_{α}E_{α}$ over any index set. Example: $\bigcup_{t∈(0,1]}(0,t)=(0,1)$ and $\bigcap_{t∈(0,1]}(0,t)=∅$.
$\mathcal P(N)$ is in bijection with the binary sequences $2^{N}$ (indicator functions), so it is uncountable.

Euclidean, Manhattan $d_{1}=Σ|x_{i}−y_{i}|$, sup $d_{∞}=\max|x_{i}−y_{i}|$, Hamming distance on binary strings, edit distance on words, shortest-path distance on a graph, great-circle distance $\arccos(p·q)$ on the sphere, and the discrete metric. Any subset inherits a restricted metric.
Open intervals in $ℝ$, open balls in $ℝ^{k}$, diamonds for the Manhattan metric, and for the discrete metric $N_{r}(x)=\{x\}$ if $r≤1$, the whole space if $r>1$.
For $E⊂X$ and $p∈X$, exactly one holds: $p$ is a limit point of $E$; $p$ is an isolated point of $E$; or $p$ is interior to $E^{c}$.
In the discrete metric every subset is both open and closed, and no set has limit points.
$[E]_{r}=\{x: d(x,y)<r$ for some $y∈E\}=\bigcup_{y∈E}N_{r}(y)$ is open. $\{q: d(q,p)>r\}$ is open, so the closed ball $\{q: d(q,p)≤r\}$ is closed.

For $E⊂X$ these are equivalent: every point is in $E$ or a limit point of $E$; $\bar E=X$; every neighborhood meets $E$; every nonempty open set meets $E$. $ℚ$, the irrationals and the dyadic rationals $k/2^{n}$ are dense in $ℝ$.
If $R=\{x_{1},x_{2},…\}$, choose closed intervals $I_{1}⊃I_{2}⊃⋯$ of positive length with $x_{n}∉I_{n}$. Their intersection contains some $x$, but $x=x_{m}$ for some $m$ and $x_{m}∉I_{m}$.
items.note: A second proof besides Cantor's diagonal argument (2.14).
Used to shrink nested cells to a point.

items.back: In an infinite set with the discrete metric, the whole space is infinite and bounded but has no limit points.

items.front: Finite sets are compact; $ℤ$ and $ℝ$ are not
items.back: Pick one cover set per point. $\{(−n,n)\}$ covers $ℤ$ (and $ℝ$) with no finite subcover.
Cover $K$ by the increasing balls $N_{n}(x)$; a finite subcover is a single ball.
items.note: Rudin only gets this inside the proof of 2.41.

items.prompt: Prove: Neighborhoods are open.
items.modelProof: Take $q∈N_{r}(p)$ and set $h=r−d(p,q)>0$. If $d(q,s)<h$, then $d(p,s) ≤ d(p,q)+d(q,s) < r$. So $N_{h}(q)⊂N_{r}(p)$.

items.prompt: Prove: Open iff complement closed.
items.modelProof: ($⇐$) Let $E^{c}$ be closed and $x∈E$. Then $x∉E^{c}$ and $x$ is not a limit point of $E^{c}$, so some neighborhood of $x$ misses $E^{c}$, i.e. lies in $E$. ($⇒$) If $x$ is a limit point of $E^{c}$, every neighborhood of $x$ meets $E^{c}$, so $x$ is not interior to $E$; since $E$ is open, $x∉E$, so $x∈E^{c}$.

items.prompt: Prove: Compact sets are closed.
items.modelProof: Let $p∉K$. For each $q∈K$ take $V_{q}=N_{r}(p)$, $W_{q}=N_{r}(q)$ with $r<d(p,q)/2$. Finitely many $W_{q_{i}}$ cover $K$; the intersection $V$ of the matching $V_{q_{i}}$ is a neighborhood of $p$ missing $K$. So $K^{c}$ is open.
items.classNote: Different cover in class; same idea.

items.prompt: Prove: Cantor's diagonal argument.
items.modelProof: Given any list $s_{1}, s_{2}, …$ of binary sequences, define $s$ by making its $n$th digit differ from the $n$th digit of $s_{n}$. Then $s≠s_{n}$ for all $n$, so no list contains every binary sequence.

items.prompt: Prove: $k$-cells are compact (bisection).
items.modelProof: If some open cover of a $k$-cell $I$ had no finite subcover, cut $I$ into $2^{k}$ subcells; one of them also has no finite subcover. Repeat to get nested cells $I_{n}$ with diameters $→0$. They share a point $x^{*}$, which lies in some open $G_{α}$ of the cover; for large $n$, $I_{n}⊂G_{α}$, a contradiction.

items.prompt: Prove: Outside the closure means inside the complement's interior.
items.modelProof: If $x∉\bar E$ then $x∉E$ and $x$ is not a limit point of $E$, so some $N_{r}(x)$ contains no point of $E$ other than possibly $x$, hence none at all. So $N_{r}(x)⊂E^{c}$ (Quiz 2, problem 15).

items.prompt: Prove that the set of polynomials with integer coefficients is countable. Deduce that the algebraic numbers are countable.
items.hint: Sort polynomials by degree; each degree class looks like $ℤ^{n+1}$.
items.modelProof: Polynomials of degree $≤ n$ correspond to $ℤ^{n+1}$, countable by 2.13. The union over $n$ is countable by 2.12. Each nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots, so the algebraic numbers are a countable union of finite sets.

items.prompt: Prove that $\mathrm{int}(E)$ is open, and that $E$ is open iff $E=\mathrm{int}(E)$.
items.modelProof: If $p$ is interior with $N_{r}(p)⊂E$, every $q∈N_{r}(p)$ has a smaller ball inside $N_{r}(p)⊂E$, so $q$ is interior too; thus $N_{r}(p)⊂\mathrm{int}E$. The second statement is the definition of open.

items.prompt: Show $d(x,y)=\dfrac{|x−y|}{1+|x−y|}$ is a metric on $ℝ$.
items.hint: The function $φ(t)=t/(1+t)$ is increasing and satisfies $φ(a+b) ≤ φ(a)+φ(b)$ for $a,b≥0$.
items.modelProof: Positivity and symmetry are clear. Triangle: $d(x,z)=φ(|x−z|) ≤ φ(|x−y|+|y−z|) ≤ φ(|x−y|)+φ(|y−z|)$, using $\frac{a+b}{1+a+b} = \frac{a}{1+a+b}+\frac{b}{1+a+b} ≤ \frac{a}{1+a}+\frac{b}{1+b}$.

items.prompt: If $K$ is compact and $F$ is closed in a metric space, prove $K∩F$ is compact.
items.modelProof: $K∩F$ is an intersection of two closed sets (2.34), hence closed, and it sits inside compact $K$, so it is compact (2.35).

items.prompt: Let $E$ be the set of $x∈[0,1]$ whose decimal expansion uses only the digits 4 and 7. Show $E$ is uncountable and compact.
items.hint: Match $E$ with binary sequences; for compactness show $E^{c}$ is open or $E$ is closed.
items.modelProof: The map sending a 4/7 sequence to $x$ is a bijection onto $E$, and 4/7 sequences correspond to binary sequences, so $E$ is uncountable (2.14). $E$ is bounded; it is closed because $E=\bigcap E_{n}$, where $E_{n}$ is the finite union of closed intervals of numbers whose first $n$ digits are 4s and 7s. Heine–Borel finishes it.

items.prompt: Prove $\overline{A∪B} = \bar A ∪ \bar B$, and show $\overline{A∩B}$ can differ from $\bar A ∩ \bar B$.
items.hint: This is Quiz 2 problems 10–11. Redo them without looking.
items.modelProof: ⊆: $\bar A∪\bar B$ is closed (finite union) and contains $A∪B$, so it contains the smallest closed superset. ⊇: $A⊂A∪B$ gives $\bar A⊂\overline{A∪B}$, same for $B$. Counterexample: $A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$.

items.prompt: From L4.2 (exercise): prove $O_{r}(p)=\{q: d(q,p)>r\}$ is open, and deduce the closed ball is closed.
items.hint: Mirror the proof that neighborhoods are open.
items.modelProof: Let $d(q,p)>r$ and $s=d(q,p)−r$. If $d(z,q)<s$, then $d(z,p)≥d(q,p)−d(q,z)>r$. So $N_{s}(q)⊂O_{r}(p)$. The closed ball is $O_{r}(p)^{c}$, closed by 2.23.

items.prompt: From L3.2: prove the Hamming distance is a metric on $\{0,1\}^{n}$.
items.hint: For the triangle inequality, compare the sets of coordinates where strings differ.
items.modelProof: Nonnegativity, $d=0$ iff equal, and symmetry are clear. If $x_{i}≠z_{i}$ then $x_{i}≠y_{i}$ or $y_{i}≠z_{i}$, so the set where $x,z$ differ is inside the union of the other two sets, giving $d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.

items.prompt: From L4.2: prove the irrationals are dense in $ℝ$.
items.hint: Use density of $ℚ$ on a shifted interval.
items.modelProof: Given $a<b$, pick rational $p$ with $a−\sqrt2<p<b−\sqrt2$. Then $p+\sqrt2∈(a,b)$ is irrational.

items.prompt: From L5.2: in the nested-interval proof that $ℝ$ is uncountable, explain how to choose $I_{n+1}⊂I_{n}$ of positive length with $x_{n+1}∉I_{n+1}$.
items.modelProof: Cut $I_{n}=[a,b]$ into thirds $[a,a+h]$, $[a+h,a+2h]$, $[a+2h,b]$. The point $x_{n+1}$ can't lie in both the first and the last third (they're disjoint), so pick one of those that misses it.

items.prompt: From L5.2: prove that every $y$ in $N_{R}(x)⊂ℝ^{k}$ satisfies $|y_{i}−x_{i}|≤R$ for each $i$, so $N_{R}(x)$ lies in a $k$-cell.
items.hint: One coordinate is at most the whole norm.

items.prompt: From L5.1: show $E=[0.1,1)$ is not compact using $V_{n}=(1/n,1−1/n)$, $n≥3$.
items.modelProof: They cover $E$ since each $x<1$ lies in $V_{n}$ once $1/n<\min(x,1−x)$. A finite union equals the largest $V_{n_{k}}$, which misses $[1−1/n_{k},1)∩E$.

items.prompt: Every closed and bounded subset of a metric space is compact.
items.explanation: Discrete metric on $ℕ$, or $\{p∈ℚ:2<p^{2}<3\}$ in $ℚ$. True in $ℝ^{k}$ (Heine–Borel).

items.prompt: $\mathrm{int}(A∪B) = \mathrm{int}A ∪ \mathrm{int}B$.
items.explanation: $A=ℚ$, $B=ℝ∖ℚ$: both interiors are empty, but $\mathrm{int}R=ℝ$. (⊇ always holds.)

items.prompt: For any set $E$ in a metric space, $E'$ is closed.
items.explanation: If $x$ is a limit point of $E'$, each $N_{r}(x)$ contains some $y∈E'$, $y≠x$; a smaller ball around $y$ inside $N_{r}(x)∖\{x\}$ contains a point of $E$. Same idea as Quiz 2 problem 9.

items.prompt: The set of all sequences of natural numbers is countable.
items.explanation: It contains the sequences using only the digits 1 and 2, which are in bijection with binary sequences (2.14). Compare Quiz 2 problem 14: eventually constant sequences are countable.

items.prompt: A subset of $ℝ$ with no limit points is finite.
If $E⊂ℝ$ is compact and nonempty, then $\sup E∈E$.
items.explanation: Compact sets are closed and bounded, and $\sup E∈\bar E=E$ (2.28).

items.prompt: Every nonempty perfect set contains an interval.
items.explanation: The Cantor set is perfect and contains no interval.

items.prompt: The union of two connected subsets of $ℝ$ that intersect is connected.
items.explanation: Both are intervals sharing a point, so their union is an interval.

items.claim: Every closed and bounded subset of a metric space is compact.
lines: Let $E$ be closed and bounded, say $E⊂N_{R}(p)$.
Then $E$ is a closed subset of the bounded set $N_{R}(p)$, and closed subsets of compact sets are compact by 2.35.
items.explanation: $N_{R}(p)$ is bounded but not compact, so 2.35 doesn't apply, and Heine–Borel is a theorem about $ℝ^{k}$ only. The claim is false (discrete metric on $ℕ$).

items.claim: Any union of closed sets is closed.
lines: Let $F=\bigcup F_{α}$ and let $p$ be a limit point of $F$.
Then $p$ is a limit point of some $F_{α}$.
items.explanation: A limit point of the union need not be a limit point of any single piece. Each $\{1/n\}$ is closed, but 0 is a limit point of the union and of none of the pieces. For finitely many pieces the step can be repaired: if $p$ is not a limit point of any $F_{i}$, the minimum of the finitely many radii gives a ball missing $F$.

lines: List the rationals in $(0,1)$ as decimals $r_{1}, r_{2}, …$.
Build $x$ whose $n$th digit differs from the $n$th digit of $r_{n}$.
Then $x$ is not on the list, contradiction.
items.explanation: The diagonal number $x$ need not be rational, so it doesn't have to be on the list. No contradiction.

items.name: $(0,1)$ and the cover $\{(1/n,1)\}$
items.details: Open cover with no finite subcover, so $(0,1)$ is not compact.

items.name: $\{1/n : n∈ℕ\}$
items.details: $E'=\{0\}$ and $(E')'=∅$ (Quiz 2 problem 8). Neither open nor closed; $E∪\{0\}$ is compact.

items.name: $ℤ$
items.details: Closed, unbounded, not compact; every point is isolated, so it has no limit points.

items.name: Discrete metric on $ℕ$
items.details: $d(p,q)=1$ for $p≠q$. $ℕ$ is closed and bounded but not compact: the cover by singletons has no finite subcover. Heine–Borel is special to $ℝ^{k}$.

items.name: $\{p∈ℚ : 2<p^{2}<3\}$ inside $ℚ$
items.details: Closed and bounded in the metric space $ℚ$, but not compact.

items.name: $\bigcap(−1/n,1/n) = \{0\}$; $\bigcup[1/n,1]=(0,1]$
items.details: Infinite intersections of open sets need not be open; infinite unions of closed sets need not be closed.

items.name: The Cantor set
items.details: Perfect, uncountable, contains no interval, and has total length 0.

items.name: $ℚ$ and the irrationals
items.details: Both dense, both have empty interior, but their union is $ℝ$. Shows $\mathrm{int}(A∪B)$ can be larger than $\mathrm{int}A∪\mathrm{int}B$.
